lesson.title: Short circuits, safety and other chemistries

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is over 1800 A at the battery's terminals, falling only as the cable adds its milliohms, when you drag the fault away from the battery.

interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A 12 V lead-acid block sits on the left, drawn as six cells in series in one case. Each cell is drawn as an emf behind a small resistance. A pair of cables runs from its terminals to the right, with a protective device at the battery end. The device can break 1 kA, an example value. A line on a bar marks it. The fault is a red link across the two cores, and you can drag it along the cable. A fault-distance slider runs from 0 m to 20 m in steps of 0.5 m. At its start, the fault sits across the terminals, just past the device. The block is a real product. Six cells at 2.1 V give it 12.6 V open circuit. It has 6.95 mΩ inside. The cable is an example. Each core has 0.5 mΩ a metre. A fault d metres away puts both cores in the loop, out and back. So the outside resistance is 1 mΩ for every metre. The fault current is the open-circuit voltage ÷ (the battery's resistance + the outside resistance). The 'Fault current' readout shows it in A. Its bar turns red while it is above the device's line. The 'Loop resistance' readout shows the total in mΩ. A charge-left slider runs from 100% down to 60% in steps of 5%. As the charge falls, the current falls in a straight line. At 60% charge it reaches 92% of the full-charge value. That line is a sketch. It stays above the measured 90%. A time trace under the cable draws the current from the moment of the fault to 20 ms. It is a sketch. It climbs to its full value by 5 ms and stays there. A 'Big string' switch swaps the block for a real 480 V string. Its loop adds up to 0.160 + 0.028 Ω. The fault slider then rests at 0 m. The readout shows 2553 A. A chemistry card below compares three cells: lead-acid, nickel-cadmium and lithium-ion. Each column gives the cell voltage, the cells in series for 24 V, the electrolyte, whether a hydrometer reads the charge, and its hazards. On a phone, the two readouts each sit on their own line. The card's three columns stack one under another. No word splits. Each show screen has under about 90 words. Each one ends on what its finished picture shows. So it reads well without the controls. Screen by screen. 0 asks a recall question. A protective device sits where the prospective fault current is 3 kA. It asks what its breaking capacity must be. First choice: at least 3 kA, the most it may have to break there. Second: at least its rated current. Third: at least the cable's current rating. The right pick says 'Still there: a device must break the biggest fault it can see where it sits.' Hint for rated current: that sets when it trips on overload, not what it can safely break. Hint for the cable: that is what the cable carries all day, far below a fault. 1 shows the 12 V block with a fault across its terminals. It reads 12.6 V open circuit and has 6.95 mΩ inside. Each cell is an emf behind a small resistance. Short the terminals, and that resistance alone limits the current. So the fault current is the open-circuit voltage ÷ the internal resistance: 12.6 ÷ 0.00695 = 1813 A. The maker lists 1814 A for this block. That is far above the device's 1 kA. It ends at 0 m with 1813 A showing. 2 says you lay a steel spanner across the terminals of the same 12 V block. It asks what flows. First choice: up to about 1800 A, held back only by the block's milliohms and the spanner. Second: very little, because 12 V is too low to push much current. Third: about 70 A, the block's ampere-hour rating. The right pick says 'That's it: 12.6 V across a few milliohms is well over a thousand amps.' Hint for too low: your body's resistance is high, so 12 V drives little current through you. A spanner's resistance is tiny. Hint for 70 A: ampere-hours say how long a battery lasts, not how hard it can push. Its Why adds that the spanner gets very hot very quickly, and can explode in a shower of molten metal that burns and can light hydrogen. 3 drags the fault along the cable. Both cable cores now join the loop. So the current is the voltage ÷ (the battery's resistance + the outside resistance). Each core has 0.5 mΩ a metre, so each metre adds 1 mΩ. At 5 m the loop is 6.95 + 5 = 11.95 mΩ. That gives 12.6 ÷ 0.01195 = 1054 A, still above the device's 1 kA. The battery's milliohms are fixed. Only the loop outside can add more. It ends at 5 m with 1054 A showing. 4 says a fault happens 10 m down the same cable. It asks for the fault current. The choices are 743 A, 1260 A and 1813 A. The right pick says 'That's it: 12.6 ÷ (0.00695 + 0.010) = 743 A.' Hint for 1260 A: that is 12.6 ÷ 0.010, the cable alone. The battery's 6.95 mΩ is in the loop too. Hint for 1813 A: that is the fault at the terminals, before the cable adds its 10 mΩ. 5 taps 'Big string'. The same rule works for a real 480 V string. The cells' resistance and the links between them set the most a battery can drive. This string's loop adds up to 0.160 + 0.028 Ω. 480 ÷ 0.188 = 2553 A, so the rule predicts about 2550 A. A real test on that string measured 2530 A. A shorted battery can give 100 to 1000 times its normal discharge current. It ends with the big string showing 2553 A. 6 says a 48 V string has 24 cells at 2.1 V, each with 1.5 mΩ inside. Its 23 links between cells add 0.1 mΩ each. These are example values. It asks for the fault current across its terminals. The choices are 1316 A, 1400 A and 33600 A. The right pick says 'That's it: 50.4 V ÷ (36 + 2.3) mΩ = 1316 A.' Hint for 1400 A: the links carry the fault current too, so their 2.3 mΩ belongs in the loop. Hint for 33600 A: in a string, one current flows through every cell. So the cells' resistances add. 7 drags the charge left from 100% down to 60%. The fault current barely moves. A cell's rested voltage falls only a little as its charge goes. The milliohms stay milliohms. In tests on real batteries, the current stayed above 90% of its full-charge value at about 60% charge. In this sketch, the block still drives 1668 A at 60%. The band under the bar marks the tests' over 90%. So a part-discharged battery can still give nearly its full fault. It ends at 60% charge with 1668 A showing. 8 says a UPS battery has run down to about 60% charge, and someone says a short on it now would be small. It asks whether that is right. First choice: no, its fault current is still over 90% of the full-charge value. Second: yes, it falls to about 60% of the full-charge fault. Third: yes, a part-charged battery holds too little energy for a big current. The right pick says 'That's it: the volts barely fall and the milliohms stay, so the current stays high.' Hint for 60%: the current follows the voltage, not the charge left. The voltage barely falls. Hint for too little energy: energy sets how long it could keep going, not how many amps flow at once. 9 shows the time trace. A battery has little inductance, so a short acts like a fault through a plain resistor. The current reaches its full value within 5 to 10 ms of the fault. The trace is marked as a sketch. The cells cannot be switched off either. Their exposed metal is always live. Switching off the charger and the loads stops their currents. The cells keep their voltage. It ends with the trace flat at 1813 A, with the fault at 0 m. 10 says you must remake a loose link between two cells in a live string. It asks what comes first. First choice: switch off the circuits on the battery, and keep metal tools off its top. Second: open the battery's main switch, and then the cells are dead. Third: nothing, because each link spans only one cell's 2.1 V. The right pick says 'That's it: switch off all circuits before connecting or disconnecting, and rest no metal on a battery.' Hint for the main switch: a switch stops current in the circuits, but the cells keep their voltage. Hint for one cell: your spanner can bridge more than one cell. Even one cell can drive over a thousand amps through metal. 11 shows the chemistry card. Other chemistries obey the same fault rule, but their cells differ. Lithium-ion brings a new hazard, thermal runaway: a cell's own heat speeds its reactions, and they make more heat. The card carries the facts. Lead-acid gives about 2 V a cell, so 24 V takes 12 cells, and a hydrometer reads a vented cell's charge. Nickel-cadmium gives 1.20 V, so 24 V takes 20 cells, and a hydrometer cannot read the charge. Both have very corrosive electrolytes and give off hydrogen on charge. A common lithium-ion type gives 3.60 V, so 7 cells make 25.2 V. Its electrolyte is a lithium salt in a flammable organic solvent. It ends on all three columns. 12, 13 and 14 mix the ideas. 12 says a nickel-cadmium battery needs its charge checked, and a hydrometer is to hand. It asks what the hydrometer will tell you. First choice: nothing about the charge, because the electrolyte is not used up in the reaction. Second: the charge, read the same way as lead-acid. Third: the charge, on a lower scale. The right pick says 'That's it: the alkali carries the current but is not used up, so its strength stays put.' Hint for the same way: lead-acid's acid is used up on discharge. That change is what a hydrometer reads. Hint for a lower scale: any scale needs a reading that changes with charge. This one does not. 13 says a 24 V emergency battery has 12 lead-acid cells at 2.1 V and 14 mΩ in total, links included. A fault 2 m down its cable adds 2 mΩ. The device there can break 1 kA. These are example values. It asks whether the device can clear the fault. First choice: yes, about 1.6 A, far below 1 kA. Second: no, about 1575 A, above 1 kA. Third: yes, at 60% charge, about 945 A, below 1 kA. The right pick says 'That's it: 25.2 V across 16 mΩ is 1575 A, more than the device can break.' Hint for 1.6 A: 16 mΩ is 0.016 Ω, so the current is a thousand times bigger. Hint for 945 A: at 60% charge it would still give over 90% of that, not 60%. 14 shows one 3.60 V cell against a 24 V line. It says a pack of 3.60 V lithium-ion cells is to replace that 24 V lead-acid battery. It asks how many cells in series it needs, and whether a hydrometer can check its charge. First choice: 7 cells, and no hydrometer. Second: 12 cells, checked with a hydrometer. Third: 20 cells, and no hydrometer. The right pick says 'That's it: 7 × 3.60 V = 25.2 V, and its cells are sealed.' Hint for 12 cells: that count suits lead-acid's 2 V a cell. Hint for 20 cells: that count suits nickel-cadmium's 1.20 V a cell.
interactive.ignores: The fault is drawn as a bolted short of no resistance. A real fault often arcs. The arc adds its own resistance and voltage drop, so a real fault current is usually somewhat lower. The block's resistance is held fixed. A real cell's changes a little with charge and temperature. The charge-left line and the time trace are sketches. The charger and any running motors would add their own current to a fault. The picture leaves them out. Each cable core is the same example size at room temperature.

explain.text:
A large battery is an emf behind a few milliohms. So almost nothing limits a short across it. It can drive thousands of amps into a fault, even part discharged. And its cells cannot be switched off. What you know about prospective fault current still holds. Only the source is new.

Short the terminals and the outside resistance falls to almost nothing. The cells' own internal resistance is then all that holds the current back. So the [[short-circuit current]] is the open-circuit voltage ÷ the internal resistance. A real 12 V 70 Ah block has 6.95 mΩ inside. Its maker lists 1814 A.[^3] Check it. Six cells at 2.1 V give 12.6 V, and 12.6 ÷ 0.00695 = 1813 A. A spanner across the terminals carries that current and gets very hot very quickly.[^10] It can explode in a shower of molten metal, which burns and can light hydrogen. Move the fault down a cable, and the cable joins the loop. The current is then V ÷ (R battery + R outside). A fault 5 m down the example cable adds 5 mΩ. The current is still 1054 A. The links between the cells add to that loop, just as the cable does. The rule holds on real batteries. For one 480 V string it predicted about 2550 A, and a test measured 2530 A.

Two things make this worse than it looks. First, the current hardly falls as the battery runs down. A rested cell's voltage falls only a little as its charge goes. The milliohms stay milliohms. In tests the current stayed above 90% of its full-charge value at about 60% charge.[^6] Second, the current arrives at once. A battery has little inductance, so a short acts like a fault through a plain resistor. The current reaches its full value within 5 to 10 ms.[^7] A battery's exposed metal is live all the time. Switching off the circuits stops their currents. But no switch makes the cells dead. So a part-discharged battery is hardly safer to work on. It can still drive nearly its full fault.

Other chemistries obey the same rule, but their cells differ. Lead-acid gives about 2 V a cell. Its acid is used up on discharge, so a hydrometer reads a vented cell's charge. A nickel-cadmium cell gives 1.20 V, so 24 V takes 20 cells. Its potassium hydroxide is not used up in the reaction, so a hydrometer tells you nothing about the charge.[^11] A common lithium-ion cell gives 3.60 V.[^9] So 7 cells make 25.2 V. Some types give less. Its electrolyte is a lithium salt in a flammable organic solvent.[^12] It needs a protection circuit to prevent [[thermal runaway]] if stressed. In thermal runaway, a cell's own heat speeds its reactions, and they make more heat. Finding a battery's earth faults is its own subject, in Insulated systems and earth faults. BS 7671 now has a new chapter covering stationary batteries. A real fault through an arc usually runs somewhat lower. **A large battery's few milliohms let it drive thousands of amps into a short, even part discharged, and its cells are always live.**

analogy.text: You know fault level at a supply transformer. Its impedance is tiny, so a fault at its terminals draws a huge current. Move the fault down a final circuit, and the cable's impedance cuts it to a fraction. A battery is that transformer. Its milliohms take the place of the transformer's impedance. The same sum gives the fault current: voltage ÷ loop impedance. And the device nearest the source faces the biggest fault.
analogy.breaks: A transformer's impedance is mostly reactance, so its fault current takes a moment to settle. You can also isolate a transformer from upstream. A battery's impedance is almost pure resistance, so its fault arrives within milliseconds. And nothing upstream can make its cells dead.

practice.text:
Use this whenever you work on, near or downstream of a battery.

**Safe way first:**
- Treat every battery as live. Its exposed metal always carries a voltage.
- Switch off all circuits before connecting or disconnecting a battery. That stops their currents. The cells stay live.
- Keep metal off the battery. Don't rest tools on top of it.
- The cells stay live, so use insulated tools. Work on one connection at a time. Cover the terminals you are not touching.
- Protect your eyes near the electrolyte. In lead-acid and nickel-cadmium cells it is sulphuric acid or potassium hydroxide. Both can permanently damage the eyes and burn the skin.
- If it splashes, wash with plenty of clean water and get medical help at once.

**To estimate a battery's fault current:**
- Find the open-circuit voltage: the cells × the volts a cell.
- Add every resistance in the loop: the cells, the links between them, and the cable out and back.
- Divide the voltage by that total. That is the battery's share of the fault.
- Add what the charger and any running motors can give.
- Check each protective device against the fault just past it, at full charge. Its DC breaking capacity at that voltage must be at least that current.

**Rule of thumb:** a shorted battery can give 100 to 1000 times its normal discharge current. A low voltage does not mean a low fault current.

**Worked example:** A 24 V emergency battery has 12 lead-acid cells at 2.1 V. It reads 25.2 V open circuit. Say its cells and links total 14 mΩ. Across its terminals, 25.2 ÷ 0.014 = 1800 A. Now put the fault 2 m down a cable. Each core has 0.5 mΩ a metre, so the cable adds 2 mΩ. Then 25.2 ÷ 0.016 = 1575 A. So a device at the battery must break at least 1800 A, plus the charger's share. These are example values. A real battery's figures come from its maker.

**Common mistakes**
- Thinking 12 V or 24 V is too low to matter. It drives little current through you. But a large battery drives over a thousand amps through a spanner.
- Thinking a part-discharged battery is safer. In tests, a battery at about 60% charge still gave over 90% of its full fault current.
- Switching off the loads and treating the cells as dead.
- Leaving the links, the cable or the battery's own resistance out of the sum.
- Reading a nickel-cadmium cell's charge with a hydrometer.

checks.label: The maker lists 1814 A short-circuit current and 6.95 mΩ for its 12 V 70 Ah block: six cells give 12.6 ÷ 0.00695 = 1813 A, within 1 A of it
A charged, rested lead-acid cell reads 2.1 V open circuit: six make the block's 12.6 V and twelve make 25.2 V
A battery's short-circuit current is estimated by dividing its open-circuit voltage by its internal resistance: with the fault at the terminals the loop is the block's 6.95 mΩ alone
The cable adds 1 mΩ a metre of route: 5 m gives 11.95 mΩ and 1054 A, still above 1 kA; 10 m gives 743 A, below it; the cable alone at 10 m would give 1260 A; the current falls with every half metre
About 2550 A was predicted for a 480 V string from 480 V ÷ (0.160 + 0.028) Ω, against 2530 A measured: the big string shows 2553 A and 188 mΩ, wherever the fault slider sits
Short-circuit current exceeded 90% of nominal even at about 60% charge: the sketch keeps 92%, so 1668 A of 1813 A at 60%, falling in a straight line
Steady maximum current was reached within 5 to 10 ms: the sketched trace starts at 0, is full by 5 ms and stays flat to 20 ms
The 48 V string: 50.4 V ÷ (36 + 2.3) mΩ = 1316 A; leaving out the links gives 1400 A, and 24 × 1400 = 33600 A
The 24 V emergency battery: 25.2 ÷ 0.016 = 1575 A 2 m down its cable and 25.2 ÷ 0.014 = 1800 A at its terminals, both above the 1 kA device
A nickel-cadmium cell's low 1.20 V needs many cells: 20 for 24 V, against 12 lead-acid cells at 2 V
A lithium-ion cell's nominal voltage is 3.60 V: 7 in series make 25.2 V, the fewest that reach 24 V
Potassium hydroxide is not used in the reaction, so the nickel-cadmium floats ride at one height, full or part charged
Each puzzle accepts only its right answer, and nothing in its picture gives the answer before Check

Every demonstration settles within 4.6 s and ends where its screen says, and every answer's motion settles within 2.5 s

applied.problem: Over-general and over-certain: 'A battery' has milliohms and drives thousands of amps only if large (bold drops 'large'); 'takes no part in the reaction' overstates the quote ('isn't used'); 3.60 V is one lithium-ion type, not all; a battery that gives out early on test is beyond the 60% data.

Electrolyte line is false for lithium-ion, just taught; '60% gives over 90%' is stated as general where the source is one test series; breaking capacity should be 'at least' and DC-rated, as screen 0 and BS 7671 put it; '12 V drives over a thousand amps' holds only for a large battery; insulated tools are standard safe practice.

Screen 9 states one test's 5 to 10 ms as a general law; screens 11 and 14 treat 3.60 V as every lithium-ion cell; screen 12 says KOH 'takes no part' where the source says it is not used up; screen 2's 1800 A ignores spanner and contact resistance; screen 7's 'cannot run its load for long' goes beyond the 60% data.
